bibl.title: Crystallography Open Database – an open-access collection of crystal structures

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: an open-access collection of published crystal structures, and the deposition machinery - identifiers, versioning, duplicate detection, validation - that lets a community keep one
span.quote: The Crystallography Open Database (COD) is an ongoing initiative by crystallographers to gather all published inorganic, metal–organic and small organic molecule structures in one database, providing a straightforward search and retrieval interface. The COD adopts an open-access model for its >80 000 structure files.

span.label: how to gather structural data that was historically split across three specialised databases into one searchable open collection, and keep it correct while it grows
span.quote: The historical fragmentation of structural data into three databases covering inorganic compounds (Inorganic Crystal Structure Database; Belsky et al., 2002), metals, alloys and intermetallics (Crystal Data for Metals Database, CRYSTMET; White et al., 2002), and organic and organometallic small molecules (Cambridge Structural Database; Allen, 2002) reflects the fact that in the past most public or private research laboratories concentrated their activity on one or the other of these very specialized topics.

span.label: the COD itself at ~80,000 entries with near-full coverage of IUCr publications, plus a deposition pipeline that is described in enough detail to be re-implemented: permanent identifiers, Subversion revisions written into the file header, a four-condition duplicate rule ending in a human
span.quote: The Crystallography Open Database (COD) is an ongoing initiative by crystallographers to gather all published inorganic, metal–organic and small organic molecule structures in one database, providing a straightforward search and retrieval interface. The COD adopts an open-access model for its >80 000 structure files.

span.label: method
span.quote: Each CIF is checked for syntax errors, using both the publicly available ‘vcif’ tool from the IUCr (McMahon, 1998) and our own CIF parser written in Perl (http://www.perl.com/; Wall et al., 2000). Syntactic errors, if any, must be corrected manually; this task is currently performed by a COD maintainer responsible for deposition.

span.label: a scientific record split across databases by historical accident rather than by anything about the objects, and the identity problems that appear when the pieces are brought back together
span.quote: The historical fragmentation of structural data into three databases covering inorganic compounds (Inorganic Crystal Structure Database; Belsky et al., 2002), metals, alloys and intermetallics (Crystal Data for Metals Database, CRYSTMET; White et al., 2002), and organic and organometallic small molecules (Cambridge Structural Database; Allen, 2002) reflects the fact that in the past most public or private research laboratories concentrated their activity on one or the other of these very specialized topics.

span.label: CIFs syntax-checked by two independent parsers, validated for required items, assigned sequential permanent numbers, scanned for duplicates against four conjunctive criteria with manual review, then committed to a Subversion repository and dumped into an SQL table
span.term: CIFs syntax-checked by two independent parsers, validated for required items, assigned sequential permanent numbers, scanned for duplicates against four conjunctive criteria with manual review, then committed to a Subversion repository and dumped into an SQL table
span.quote: When all quality checks are passed, the existing COD database is scanned for duplicates. Duplicate structures are as a rule not deposited into the COD. A structure is considered a potential duplicate if its cell constants are within 0.5 Å and cell angles within 1.2° of any existing entry, the summary chemical formulas match, and both structures have been published in the same paper. If pressure and temperature are specified, these are also checked, and structures are considered duplicates only if they were measured under identical conditions. All potential duplicates are flagged and reviewed manually.

span.label: a permanent identifier is what makes citation possible and therefore must never change; a file that can never change cannot be corrected. The COD keeps the number fixed and versions the file underneath it, then writes both the revision and the repository address INTO the file, so that a copy taken away still says which state of which record it is
span.term: two numbers because one cannot do both jobs
span.quote: Since the COD identifier of a structure, once assigned, remains unchanged, a problem might arise when a deposited COD file needs to be changed for some reason, say, a syntax or data error must be corrected after the deposition. Currently, we have adopted a version control system called Subversion (Collins-Sussman et al., 2008). Each change of any COD file is recorded in a central COD repository, and the new version of the file automatically gets a new revision number. These numbers, along with the COD repository address, are inserted by the software into the COD file header.

span.label: two measurements can agree to 0.5 A and 1.2 degrees and still be separate scientific facts; the COD only calls them duplicates if they also came from the same paper and the same pressure and temperature, and even then a person decides. The object does not determine its own key
span.quote: When all quality checks are passed, the existing COD database is scanned for duplicates. Duplicate structures are as a rule not deposited into the COD. A structure is considered a potential duplicate if its cell constants are within 0.5 Å and cell angles within 1.2° of any existing entry, the summary chemical formulas match, and both structures have been published in the same paper. If pressure and temperature are specified, these are also checked, and structures are considered duplicates only if they were measured under identical conditions. All potential duplicates are flagged and reviewed manually.

span.label: each CIF is given a full copy of the available bibliographic information rather than a pointer to it, so that the file can be processed and stored independently - the cost is duplication, and the benefit is that a file removed from the database is still interpretable
span.term: a record made self-contained on purpose
span.quote: Each separate CIF is given a full copy of available bibliographic information, so that it can be further processed and stored independently.

span.label: a structure on hold is present in the database with its cell constants, composition, symmetry and authorship visible and its COD number issued, while the coordinates - the part that could be scooped - are withheld until publication or one year, whichever comes first
span.term: an embargo that splits the record rather than hiding it
span.quote: The atomic coordinates themselves, however, will not be released to the public until either the publication describing them appears, the authors inform the COD team that the coordinates should be released, or one year elapses from the original deposition of the CIFs. If the structure is not published within one year, an e-mail will be sent to the depositing author asking whether the structure should be released or withdrawn.

span.label: the main functional limitation is the absence of a substructure search engine, because the chemical connectivity is not represented in the stored data
span.quote: At present, one of the main limitations of the functionality of the COD is the absence of a substructure search engine. In organic and metal–organic chemistry, the best way of defining such similarity is generally the presence of a common group of atoms chemically linked in the same way: this is what we call a ‘substructure’.

span.label: chemical and hydrogen bond information is preserved only if the original file carried it, and is never inferred from the structure
span.quote: We check and, when possible, restore systematic and trivial names of the reported chemical compounds and their formulas (IUPAC, structural and summary), since this information is vital for identification of the material. Information about chemical and hydrogen bonds is preserved in the COD CIFs if present in the original data file, but is not otherwise inferred from the structure.

span.label: the deposition procedure has two manual steps - number assignment and error checking - and the number of determined structures is growing exponentially
span.quote: A current challenge for all crystallographic databases, including the COD, is an exponential increase in the number of determined structural data entries. Fortunately, there is plenty of room to improve the efficiency of the COD deposition procedure. The current procedure involves a step in which a COD number is assigned by COD coordinator, and a step where the structures are checked by human depositors for possible errors. Both steps can be automated and parallelized.

span.label: bibliographic information may fall back as far as the names of the directories the files arrived in
span.quote: Bibliographic information is taken either from the data sections of the CIFs, from the data_global sections, or from auxiliary files in BibTeX (Patashnik, 2003) or PubMed XML format (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/query/static/overview.html). As a last resort, the bibliographic information may be taken from the names of the directories containing CIFs, which are then chosen to reflect journal, year and journal issue, or the name of the donating person and laboratory.

span.label: one centralised repository is the authoritative source, and decentralisation is described as possible rather than done
span.quote: The open-access nature of the COD and the PCOD permits the creation of numerous mirrors of the COD and the PCOD. At present, three mirrors are available at http://cod.ibt.lt/, http://cod.ensicaen.fr/ and http://nanocrystallography.org/. Currently, one centralized repository is kept as an authoritative source of data, but with the growth of the databases a decentralized implementation is possible.

span.label: persistent URLs for deposited data are planned rather than in place
span.quote: To facilitate the use of the COD as a reference database, it is planned that all data published in the COD will be assigned persistent URLs. Thus, any structure deposited in the COD should be available as http://www.crystallography.net/cif/〈COD number〉, e.g. http://www.crystallography.net/cif/1000000.cif.

span.label: software version control - Subversion, revision numbers, change logs, checkout of prior states - carried from programming practice into the curation of a scientific data record
span.quote: Since the COD identifier of a structure, once assigned, remains unchanged, a problem might arise when a deposited COD file needs to be changed for some reason, say, a syntax or data error must be corrected after the deposition. Currently, we have adopted a version control system called Subversion (Collins-Sussman et al., 2008). Each change of any COD file is recorded in a central COD repository, and the new version of the file automatically gets a new revision number. These numbers, along with the COD repository address, are inserted by the software into the COD file header.

span.label: bulk distribution protocols from system administration - rsync, tarballs, anonymous repository checkout - used so that the database can be taken away entire rather than queried a record at a time
span.quote: For anybody who wishes to use the COD and the PCOD databases, the collected files are presented using standard open protocols and formats. The database can be searched online on the COD server using a simple web-based search form, and the structural results can be downloaded either one by one or in a compressed .zip file. Alternatively, the whole collection of the COD files and database tables can be downloaded from the COD web site (using the http protocol) as a compressed .zip, .tar.gz or .tar.bz2 file, or updated via an rsync protocol (http://samba.anu.edu.au/rsync/) from rsync://www.crystallography.net/cod-cif and rsync://www.crystallography.net/pcod-cif so that the files can be used and examined on a user’s local machine.

span.label: every change to every file recorded in a central Subversion repository, with the revision and repository address written into the file header by software
span.note: eliminates: a silent edit - without the revision in the file, a corrected record and its predecessor are indistinguishable once either has been copied away · outcome: held
span.quote: Since the COD identifier of a structure, once assigned, remains unchanged, a problem might arise when a deposited COD file needs to be changed for some reason, say, a syntax or data error must be corrected after the deposition. Currently, we have adopted a version control system called Subversion (Collins-Sussman et al., 2008). Each change of any COD file is recorded in a central COD repository, and the new version of the file automatically gets a new revision number. These numbers, along with the COD repository address, are inserted by the software into the COD file header.

span.label: a four-condition duplicate scan - cell constants, angles, formula and same paper, plus pressure and temperature when given - with every candidate flagged for a person
span.note: eliminates: numeric closeness alone deciding identity, and an automatic merge removing a second independent determination of the same compound · outcome: held
span.quote: When all quality checks are passed, the existing COD database is scanned for duplicates. Duplicate structures are as a rule not deposited into the COD. A structure is considered a potential duplicate if its cell constants are within 0.5 Å and cell angles within 1.2° of any existing entry, the summary chemical formulas match, and both structures have been published in the same paper. If pressure and temperature are specified, these are also checked, and structures are considered duplicates only if they were measured under identical conditions. All potential duplicates are flagged and reviewed manually.

span.label: the whole collection, the database dumps and the web scripts published for anonymous checkout, so that any user can reconstitute the database and its logs locally
span.note: eliminates: the maintainers being the only witnesses to what the database contains and what was changed in it · outcome: held
span.quote: Finally, the COD and PCOD CIFs, database dumps and web scripts are available for anonymous checkouts from the COD Subversion server (svn://www.crystallography.net/cod and svn://www.crystallography.net/pcod). From this server an interested user can reconstitute locally the whole COD database and the web site for local searches, and also browse COD deposition logs and retrieve older revisions, should they be necessary.

span.label: each CIF checked for syntax by TWO independent parsers - the IUCr `vcif` tool and a COD-written Perl parser
span.note: eliminates: syntax errors in a deposited CIF, and the use of two independent parsers means an error has to be missed twice to get through · outcome: held
span.quote: Each CIF is checked for syntax errors, using both the publicly available ‘vcif’ tool from the IUCr (McMahon, 1998) and our own CIF parser written in Perl (http://www.perl.com/; Wall et al., 2000). Syntactic errors, if any, must be corrected manually; this task is currently performed by a COD maintainer responsible for deposition.

span.label: validation that required data items - cell parameters, symmetry, bibliography - are present before deposition
span.note: eliminates: depositions missing cell parameters, symmetry or bibliography - and note the verb: the CIFs `CAN BE` validated. The capability is described; the paper does not say it was run · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: The CIFs now can be validated to check whether all necessary data items such as cell parameters, symmetry or bibliography are present.

span.label: a fallback chain for bibliographic information ending, as a last resort, at the directory names the files arrived in
span.note: eliminates: unattributed structures - though the paper is candid that the last resort is the directory name, which is the weakest link in the chain it describes · outcome: held
span.quote: Bibliographic information is taken either from the data sections of the CIFs, from the data_global sections, or from auxiliary files in BibTeX (Patashnik, 2003) or PubMed XML format (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/query/static/overview.html). As a last resort, the bibliographic information may be taken from the names of the directories containing CIFs, which are then chosen to reflect journal, year and journal issue, or the name of the donating person and laboratory.

span.label: each CIF given a full copy of the bibliographic information rather than a reference to it, so it can be processed independently
span.note: eliminates: a record that cannot be interpreted once separated from the collection it arrived in · outcome: held
span.quote: Each separate CIF is given a full copy of available bibliographic information, so that it can be further processed and stored independently.

span.label: an on-hold deposition status releasing metadata and a COD number while withholding coordinates until publication or one year
span.note: eliminates: depositors withholding structures altogether for fear of being scooped, at the cost of a delay the policy bounds · outcome: held
span.quote: The atomic coordinates themselves, however, will not be released to the public until either the publication describing them appears, the authors inform the COD team that the coordinates should be released, or one year elapses from the original deposition of the CIFs. If the structure is not published within one year, an e-mail will be sent to the depositing author asking whether the structure should be released or withdrawn.

span.label: chemical and hydrogen bond information preserved from the source file and never inferred from the structure
span.note: eliminates: a structure that cannot be identified as the compound it is, and bond information silently re-derived from geometry rather than taken from the depositor · outcome: held
span.quote: We check and, when possible, restore systematic and trivial names of the reported chemical compounds and their formulas (IUPAC, structural and summary), since this information is vital for identification of the material. Information about chemical and hydrogen bonds is preserved in the COD CIFs if present in the original data file, but is not otherwise inferred from the structure.

span.label: the claim that several dozen contributors are enough to provide qualified peer review for incoming structures
span.note: eliminates: unreviewed structures reaching the database - conditional on adequate software and on enough volunteers, neither of which the paper claims to have · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: Finally, the structures still requiring human attention can be checked and edited in parallel by numerous COD reviewers all over the world, provided there is adequate software and enough volunteers participate in COD maintenance. Currently, the number of people contributing or willing to contribute to the development of the COD amounts to several dozen, apparently enough to provide qualified peer-review for the incoming structures.

The COD adopts an open-access model for its >80 000 structure files.

span.quote: The historical fragmentation of structural data into three databases covering inorganic compounds (Inorganic Crystal Structure Database; Belsky et al., 2002), metals, alloys and intermetallics (Crystal Data for Metals Database, CRYSTMET; White et al., 2002), and organic and organometallic small molecules (Cambridge Structural Database; Allen, 2002) reflects the fact that in the past most public or private research laboratories concentrated their activity on one or the other of these very specialized topics.

span.label: two entries being the SAME STRUCTURE - AS THE COD DEFINES IT: cell constants within 0.5 A, angles within 1.2 degrees, formulas matching, same paper, same pressure and temperature, and then a human agrees
span.quote: When all quality checks are passed, the existing COD database is scanned for duplicates. Duplicate structures are as a rule not deposited into the COD. A structure is considered a potential duplicate if its cell constants are within 0.5 Å and cell angles within 1.2° of any existing entry, the summary chemical formulas match, and both structures have been published in the same paper. If pressure and temperature are specified, these are also checked, and structures are considered duplicates only if they were measured under identical conditions. All potential duplicates are flagged and reviewed manually.

span.label: two entries being the SAME STRUCTURE - AS THE COD DELIBERATELY DOES NOT: a redetermination at higher precision or under different conditions gets a NEW identifier rather than replacing the old one
span.quote: Each structure deposited in the COD and the PCOD gets a unique seven-digit number, a (P)COD identifier. If a structure of a compound is redetermined, with higher precision or under different conditions, it will be deposited in the (P)COD under a new (P)COD number.

span.label: a COD record's identity - THE COD NUMBER: permanent, assigned once, and never changed even when the file it names is corrected
span.quote: Since the COD identifier of a structure, once assigned, remains unchanged, a problem might arise when a deposited COD file needs to be changed for some reason, say, a syntax or data error must be corrected after the deposition. Currently, we have adopted a version control system called Subversion (Collins-Sussman et al., 2008). Each change of any COD file is recorded in a central COD repository, and the new version of the file automatically gets a new revision number. These numbers, along with the COD repository address, are inserted by the software into the COD file header.

span.label: a COD record's identity - THE REVISION NUMBER: changes on every edit, is written into the file header by software, and is what makes any previous state recoverable
span.quote: There is a publicly accessible interface to the COD that allows older revisions of any file to be extracted and the COD change logs recorded by COD maintainers to be read. Having a COD number and the revision number of a file, it is always possible to restore a previous version of that file.

span.label: a deposited structure's visibility - UNDER THE ON-HOLD FLAG: cell constants, composition, symmetry and authorship are public and searchable
span.quote: For researchers who wish to publish their structure-related work, most journals require the deposition of structures with a crystallographic database and ask for the database accession number as proof of deposition. For such structures, a special deposition status, ‘on hold until publication’, will be introduced. The structures submitted to the COD with the ‘on hold’ flag will be included in the COD SQL database where their cell constants, composition, symmetry and authorship will be indicated. A COD number will be assigned to the structure and returned to the author, and will be visible through the search interface of the COD.

span.label: a deposited structure's visibility - THE COORDINATES UNDER THE SAME FLAG: withheld until publication, or release by the authors, or one year
span.quote: The atomic coordinates themselves, however, will not be released to the public until either the publication describing them appears, the authors inform the COD team that the coordinates should be released, or one year elapses from the original deposition of the CIFs. If the structure is not published within one year, an e-mail will be sent to the depositing author asking whether the structure should be released or withdrawn.

span.label: critiques → the historical three-way split of structural data across inorganic, metals and organic databases, which reflected how laboratories used to specialise rather than anything about the compounds
span.quote: The historical fragmentation of structural data into three databases covering inorganic compounds (Inorganic Crystal Structure Database; Belsky et al., 2002), metals, alloys and intermetallics (Crystal Data for Metals Database, CRYSTMET; White et al., 2002), and organic and organometallic small molecules (Cambridge Structural Database; Allen, 2002) reflects the fact that in the past most public or private research laboratories concentrated their activity on one or the other of these very specialized topics.

span.label: extends → the IUCr's 2007 decision to make CIFs from its journals freely available to all databases, which is what let the COD download new structures routinely
span.quote: In September 2007, the IUCr Executive Committee decided that the CIFs associated with structural papers published in IUCr journals should be made freely available to all databases, including the COD, giving the COD permission to routinely download new files from the IUCr site.

If pressure and temperature are specified, these are also checked, and structures are considered duplicates only if they were measured under identical conditions. All potential duplicates are flagged and reviewed manually.

span.label: a common group of atoms chemically linked in the same way - the paper's definition of chemical similarity, and the thing the database cannot search for
span.quote: At present, one of the main limitations of the functionality of the COD is the absence of a substructure search engine. In organic and metal–organic chemistry, the best way of defining such similarity is generally the presence of a common group of atoms chemically linked in the same way: this is what we call a ‘substructure’.

span.label: angstroms - the cell-constant tolerance inside which two entries become duplicate candidates
span.quote: When all quality checks are passed, the existing COD database is scanned for duplicates. Duplicate structures are as a rule not deposited into the COD. A structure is considered a potential duplicate if its cell constants are within 0.5 Å and cell angles within 1.2° of any existing entry, the summary chemical formulas match, and both structures have been published in the same paper. If pressure and temperature are specified, these are also checked, and structures are considered duplicates only if they were measured under identical conditions. All potential duplicates are flagged and reviewed manually.

span.label: degrees - the cell-angle tolerance in the same rule
span.quote: When all quality checks are passed, the existing COD database is scanned for duplicates. Duplicate structures are as a rule not deposited into the COD. A structure is considered a potential duplicate if its cell constants are within 0.5 Å and cell angles within 1.2° of any existing entry, the summary chemical formulas match, and both structures have been published in the same paper. If pressure and temperature are specified, these are also checked, and structures are considered duplicates only if they were measured under identical conditions. All potential duplicates are flagged and reviewed manually.

span.label: the length of a COD identifier, assigned once and never changed
span.quote: Each structure deposited in the COD and the PCOD gets a unique seven-digit number, a (P)COD identifier. If a structure of a compound is redetermined, with higher precision or under different conditions, it will be deposited in the (P)COD under a new (P)COD number.

span.label: revision number
span.quote: Since the COD identifier of a structure, once assigned, remains unchanged, a problem might arise when a deposited COD file needs to be changed for some reason, say, a syntax or data error must be corrected after the deposition. Currently, we have adopted a version control system called Subversion (Collins-Sussman et al., 2008). Each change of any COD file is recorded in a central COD repository, and the new version of the file automatically gets a new revision number. These numbers, along with the COD repository address, are inserted by the software into the COD file header.
